title: The launch-day 429s
scenario: A company runs a support assistant on the Claude API. A nightly backfill job shares the same organization. After a launch email the team reads its logs (exhibit) and has to fix four problems before the next send.
exhibit:
(made-up example data)

LOG 1: 09:01 to 09:04, live answers
  traffic:       20 requests/min -> 800 requests/min in 2 minutes
  org limit:     5,000 requests/min
  09:03  429 rate_limit_error, retry-after: 7
         anthropic-ratelimit-requests-remaining: 4,200
         anthropic-ratelimit-input-tokens-remaining: 1,650,000
         anthropic-ratelimit-output-tokens-remaining: 310,000

LOG 2: 23:10, nightly backfill
  workspace:     Default (live chat and backfill both run here)
  backfill:      200 workers in parallel, no delay
  23:10  live chat requests get 429 rate_limit_error

LOG 3: 02:40, summary job
  429 rate_limit_error
  details.error_code: enforced_spend_limit_reached
  retry-after header: none
  job behaviour: 6 attempts with backoff, then fail

LOG 4: retry settings
  SDK client:    default retries (2)
  our wrapper:   retries 5 times after each failed SDK call

questions.prompt: In log 1, 4,200 of 5,000 requests were still left, yet a 429 came. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The headers are not reliable, so the 4,200 value means nothing.
options.explanation: The header shows the remaining requests and is the real figure. It tells you the request limit was not used up.

options.text: A sharp rise in usage can hit acceleration limits below the stated limits.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs warn that a sharp increase in usage can cause 429 errors from acceleration limits. Ramp up gradually.

options.text: 5,000 per minute is enforced at about 83 per second, and 800 is above that.
options.explanation: 800 per minute is about 13 per second, far below 83. The burst rule is real, but it does not explain this log.

options.text: It is the monthly spend cap, which also returns 429 with a retry-after header.
options.explanation: A spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header and carries the error code enforced_spend_limit_reached. This one has retry-after: 7.

questions.prompt: In log 2, the backfill makes live chat fail. Which fix keeps chat safe?

options.text: Add a second API key in the same workspace for the backfill.
options.explanation: Limits are set per organization and workspace, not per key. A second key in the same workspace shares the same room.

options.text: Let the live chat retry more times, so it gets through eventually.
options.explanation: More retries add load, and failed requests count toward the limit. The backfill still takes all the room.

options.text: Set a lower limit on the Default workspace, where both jobs run.
options.explanation: The Claude docs say you can't set limits on the default workspace. The jobs have to be in separate workspaces first.

options.text: Move the backfill to its own workspace with a lower rate limit.
options.explanation: Right. Workspace limits protect other workspaces from overuse. Organization-wide limits still apply, so cut the backfill's parallel workers too.

questions.prompt: In log 3, what should the summary job do with this 429?

options.text: Stop retrying and alert a person to raise the limit.
options.explanation: Right. A spend-cap 429 has no retry-after and keeps failing until access resumes. Retries only add noise.

options.text: Retry with a longer backoff, because every 429 clears in time.
options.explanation: This 429 does not clear until access resumes, which can be days away. Longer waits do not change that.

options.text: Send the same request with another API key in the same organization.
options.explanation: The spend cap applies to the whole organization, so a different key hits the same wall.

options.text: Add random jitter to the six attempts so they spread out.
options.explanation: Jitter helps with temporary limits, where clients retry at the same moment. It cannot lift a spend cap.

questions.prompt: Using log 4, at most how many API requests can one failing user action send?

options.explanation: That counts only the wrapper's tries: 1 first try plus 5 retries. Each of those tries is itself several SDK requests.
That adds the SDK's 2 retries to the wrapper's 5 and the first try. The two layers multiply; they do not add.

Right. The wrapper makes 6 tries (1 plus 5). Each try is up to 3 SDK requests (1 plus 2). 6 times 3 is 18. Use one retry layer and cap total time. The OpenAI docs say the same: disable SDK retries or count them, so nested loops don't multiply requests.
That would be 7 wrapper tries of 3 requests each. The wrapper makes 6 tries (1 plus 5), so the total is 18.
